get.description:
Authoritative server clock for value-granting time math on the client
(the Auto-Opener). The client anchors its idle catch-up to this instead of
the device clock — otherwise a user could wind their phone forward, reopen
for a free instant catch-up, wind it back, and repeat. Public, no auth,
uncached: always returns live epoch milliseconds.

post.description:
One ad impression.

`ad_type` is 'rewarded' (a user-initiated rewarded video) or 'banner'
(the loading-screen MREC). Anything else — including a missing field,
which is what pre-1.0.10 clients send — is stored as 'rewarded', so an
older install keeps landing in the series it always did rather than in a
third bucket nothing reads.

One raw AdMob SDK signal — see the ad_signal_events table comment.

Deliberately lenient: an unknown `signal` is dropped with ok:true rather
than 400'd. These are fire-and-forget from the client and nothing retries,
so a strict server would just lose data whenever a newer build reports a
signal this deployment hasn't been taught about — and the client can't
tell the difference between "rejected" and "delivered" anyway.

get.description:
Why ad loads failed, grouped and counted, newest `hours` (max 72, the
raw rows' lifetime). One GROUP BY over a time-bounded range of the
created_at index — the shape the 2026-08-13 outage note demands. Sync
`def`, so it runs in the threadpool.

Only rows from 1.1.3+ carry `fail_detail`; older clients' failures show
up with detail null, which is itself useful (how much is unexplained).

post.description:
Logged when a real Google Play purchase completes successfully.
The app calls this from the `PurchaseStatus.purchased` branch only —
dev-bypass / restored entitlements are NOT logged so the dashboard
counts only money-true sales. `product_id` is the Play Store product
id (e.g. cs2_case_sim_boost_bundle).

Receipt verification: v1.0.4+ clients also send `purchase_token`
(the value from `PurchaseDetails.verificationData.serverVerificationData`).
When present we verify against Google's androidpublisher API and
return 403 if the token is fake / cancelled / refunded. Pre-v1.0.4
clients omit the token; we accept those for backwards compatibility
until v1.0.4 dominates the install base (then flip to strict mode —
see CLAUDE.md 'Half-finished features').

Synchronous purchase-time receipt verification. The client calls
this from the `PurchaseStatus.purchased` (and `restored`) branches
BEFORE granting the entitlement. Returns `ok=True` only if Google
confirms the token, OR if we hit a transient error (fail-open with
`fail_open: true` so the client still applies the boost — paying
users shouldn't lose entitlements to an upstream outage).

On `ok=True` the client stores `token_hash` locally and sends it
back on every startup via /api/entitlements/verify, where any
mismatch triggers a revoke.

How many cloud-save loads this player has left: `{ok, limit,
window_days, used, remaining, next_available_ms}`. Read-only; the load
dialog shows it before the player decides.

Spends one load, or refuses: `{ok: true, ...status}` /
`{ok: false, reason: "limit_reached", ...status}` (HTTP 200 — a business
rule, so a stable slug the client branches on).

Support: give one player their loads back. `{device_id}` → how many
loads were cleared. The device id comes from in-app feedback, as for
`/api/admin/gift`.

Startup batch check. Client sends `claimed`: a map of
`{product_id: token_hash}` describing which entitlements its local
state thinks it owns. For each entry we check our authoritative
`verified_entitlements` table; mismatches (no row / different hash /
refunded) go into the `revoke` list and the client revokes them.

Sentinel hash value `"__missing__"` lets the client say "I claim this
flag but I have no token for it" (typical for v1.0.5 → v1.0.6
upgraders before restorePurchases has run, or for LP fake flags
that never had a real token). These always end up in the revoke
list because no verified row matches `__missing__`.

Logged whenever the client falls back to the 25s "Reward Loading"
dialog because AdMob returned no fill (or the loaded ad failed to
show). `completed` is true if the user waited the full 25s and got
the reward, false if they cancelled. Used to compute fill rate on
the dashboard.

Logged whenever the client claims a quest reward — agent story
quest, daily-pool quest, or case-collection contract. Powers the
"User progress" dashboard panel.

Body: { device_id, quest_type, quest_id, tier? }
  quest_type — one of: 'agent' | 'pool' | 'collection'
  quest_id   — QuestDef.id / PoolQuestDef.id / case id
  tier       — only meaningful for 'pool' (0-based tier the player
               just completed). Defaults to 0 for other types.

get.description:
Dashboard analytics — all key metrics. Requires Bearer token.

Reads the payload the background refresher already built. This handler
does NO aggregation of its own unless the stored copy is missing or very
stale, so it normally returns in milliseconds however heavy the payload
is to produce.

Optional `?version=` filters the top-balances list.
`?profile=1` forces a fresh build and returns per-query timings instead.

Per-device stats. Requires Bearer token. Powers the user-detail
modal on the dashboard's Users tab — bundles the users-row data
with aggregations from ad_events, purchase_events, and
quest_claim_events so the popup shows the full picture in one
request.
Daily, monthly or yearly totals of the analytics (Phase 3, step 3).

Return daily breakdown for the last N days (max 90).
Event-based metrics (new users, ads, battles, gifts, friendships,
referral redemptions) are queried from the underlying event tables —
fully retroactive.
Cumulative metrics (total_users, balance) come from daily_snapshots.
List all device IDs and their FCM token status. Requires Bearer token.

How many pushes a user receives after closing the app for good.

Cohort: devices whose `last_seen` is between `min_dark_days` and
`max_dark_days` ago — dark long enough for every one-shot cooldown to have
fired, recent enough that `notification_log` (pruned at 30 days) still has
the rows. Counts only pushes sent AFTER that device's last_seen, so it is
literally "what we sent someone who never came back".

Read `per_device` as the answer: `avg`/`max` is the push load one churned
user carries, and `by_type` says which feature is generating it.

⚠️ **`def`, not `async def`, and that is load-bearing.** FastAPI runs an
`async def` handler ON the event loop, so the blocking SQLite work below
would stall every other request in the process for its whole duration. The
first version of this endpoint was `async def` and looped one query per
device: at ~9,500 devices that pinned the event loop long enough to take
the entire API down (2026-08-13) — /api/flags, /api/prices and the
dashboard all timed out while the machine still reported healthy, and it
needed a machine restart because killing the client curl leaves the
server-side request running. A sync `def` is handed to the threadpool
instead, so a slow admin query can only ever be slow.

⚠️ **Aggregate SQL, never a per-device loop.** Two GROUP BYs replaced
~9,500 round trips. Any new admin analytic here must do the same — this
database is on a machine whose RAM is the binding constraint (see the
`plinko_debug` note by the schema), so N+1 over the user table is never
survivable, threadpool or not.

WHEN each post-churn push lands, measured from the device's last_seen.

Same cohort as `/api/admin/churn-pushes`, but reporting the delay rather
than the count, so the theoretical schedule (4h supply drop, 24h ad case,
27h auto-opener, next-midnight daily offer, 47h30m gift) can be checked
against what devices were actually sent. Hours, per type, with percentiles.

`last_seen` is the last 60s heartbeat, so every delay here is accurate to
within a minute of the app actually closing.

Sync `def` + one query on purpose — see the warning on
`admin_churn_pushes`.

Per-SKU: how many real buyers have a `verified_entitlements` row.

This is the pre-flight check before widening `_buildClaimedMap` on the
client. A product the client starts claiming will be REVOKED for any buyer
the server can't prove, so `uncovered` is exactly the population that would
lose what they paid for on their next launch. It must be 0 (or explained)
before shipping a claim-side change for that SKU.

`covered_fail_open` is called out separately: those rows exist but were
written when Google was unreachable, so they prove only that we saw a
token, not that Google blessed it. They still satisfy the startup check
(it compares hashes, not `fail_open`), so they are safe — but a future
strict mode that ignores them would revoke this group.

Forensics on `/api/iap/verify` rejections — the Lucky-Patcher attempt log.

The `fake_purchases` block in /api/analytics answers "how many, which SKU".
This answers the three questions that block actually deciding anything:

  * **`window`** — one row per offending device over the last `days`, with
    the reason breakdown and the DISTINCT products tried. That ratio is
    what separates a scripted attack from the ordinary case: LP fakes the
    purchase stream, `restorePurchases()` runs on every launch, and each
    launch replays every faked SKU as `restored` → one rejection per faked
    product per launch. So `attempts ≈ launches × distinct_products` with
    no human retrying anything.
  * **`converted`** — devices with BOTH a rejection and a real row in
    `purchase_events`. `first_real_after_first_fake` says which came
    first, which is the difference between "tried to pirate, gave up, paid"
    and "paid once, then started faking the rest".
  * **`by_reason`** — the `detail` tag from `_verify_play_purchase`.
    `http_400` / `http_404` are Google saying the token is not real;
    anything else is a state or transient signal and is NOT an attacker.

Sales breakdown for a selectable window: "all" (default) or a specific
"YYYY-MM" month (NL tz). Mirrors the all_time block in /api/analytics —
total, unique buyers, per-product and per-country counts, and era/region-
aware revenue — so the dashboard's Sales card can switch period without
bloating the main payload.

Top spenders by REAL (net-of-Play-fee) EUR revenue across the entire
purchase_events history. Aggregates every recorded purchase per device and
prices each basket through `_sales_totals` (the same era/region-aware path
the dashboard revenue tiles use), then returns the highest-spending
devices. Admin only.

post.description:
Backfill / overwrite authoritative daily gross revenue from Play
Console exports. Used to seed the sales chart with real Play-Console
numbers (which include refunds, currency conversion, and any sales
the client-side tracker missed).

Body:
  { "rows": [ { "date": "YYYY-MM-DD", "revenue": 12.34, "notes": "..." }, ... ] }
or just a bare list:
  [ { "date": "...", "revenue": ..., "notes": "..." }, ... ]

INSERT OR REPLACE per row — safe to re-run with updated data.
Returns count of rows written. Rows with missing/unparseable
date or revenue are skipped silently rather than aborting the
whole batch.
Send a test notification to a device. Requires Bearer token.

get.description:
Diagnostic: are the re-engagement FCM pushes actually firing?

Aggregates `notification_log` (every _send_notification call records a row
with type + status: sent / failed / token_expired) over all-time / 7d / 24h,
plus FCM-token coverage and the pending-cooldown queue. Read-only, admin
token required.

Serve current skin prices JSON. Fetched by the app on every startup.

1.1.3+ clients send `If-None-Match` with the ETag of the copy they cached,
and get a bodiless 304 when it is still current — prices refresh once a
day, so that is nearly every launch, where the full answer is ~285 KB
compressed. Older clients send no header and get the 200 they always did.

Sync `def` so the occasional reload from disk runs in the threadpool, not
on the event loop.

post.description: Manually trigger a price refresh. Requires Bearer token.

get.description:
Admin: live RTP (EV / price) for every priced black market case.

Alert-only monitor for the dashboard. No SQLite, no per-row DB work — pure
in-memory compute over the cached price feed — so a plain `def` on the
threadpool is correct and can't stall the event loop.

post.description:
Erase everything this backend holds for one device.

Backs the in-app DELETE ACCOUNT button. Required by App Store Guideline
5.1.1(v) for anything that looks like an account — this app has no login,
but it does keep a persistent server-side profile, a friends graph and a
referral tree under `device_id`, which a reviewer will read as one. It is
also what makes the privacy policy's erasure promise true rather than
aspirational.

**Auth: `device_id` is the credential**, the same trust model as
`/api/analytics/heartbeat` and every other endpoint here. Knowing an id
lets you delete that device's data — but an id is a 32-char local random
that never appears in any payload sent to another player (the friends API
deliberately addresses people by opaque row ids for exactly this reason),
so it is not obtainable from inside the app.

**Two deliberate exceptions to "delete everything":**

1. `blacklisted_devices` rows SURVIVE. Erasure must not be a
   one-tap way to clear an anti-cheat sanction. The row holds no personal
   data beyond the id itself, and retaining it is a legitimate-interest
   fraud-prevention measure. (Reinstalling already rotates the id and
   evades the blacklist — that hole exists regardless and is not widened
   here, because this endpoint does NOT rotate the caller's id.)

2. `purchase_events` rows are ANONYMISED, not deleted — `device_id` is
   overwritten with a sentinel. These are financial records behind the
   revenue dashboard and the per-country net-value maths; deleting them
   would silently rewrite historical revenue every time somebody erased
   their account. Retention of transaction records is a recognised
   erasure exemption, and stripping the id satisfies the intent: the row
   survives as a sale, not as a person.

Erasing a device the backend has never seen is a no-op that still returns
`ok: true`. **But a second erasure inside `account_delete_cooldown_hours`
is refused** with `{ok: false, reason: "too_soon", retry_after_s}` — see
`_claim_erasure_slot`. The client reads `ok`, never just the status, so a
refusal shows "delete failed" and leaves the phone's save alone.

Soft-hide / un-hide a feedback row. Admin-only. Body:
`{ "hidden": true | false }`. Returns 404 if no such row.
Increment the total supply drop claim counter.

Record one event-wheel spin for the Right Now panel.
Body: { device_id, won }. `won` truthy = a jackpot spin.

Record one Auto-Opener claim for the dashboard's tuning panel.
Body: { device_id, value:$, item_count, cases_opened }.
`value` is the total banked that claim (kept items + auto-sold pile).

get.description: Get total supply drop claims. Requires Bearer token.

post.description:
App-side claim. Returns the actual amount the client should add to
its balance, or 0 if there's nothing pending. No auth — the device_id
is the credential (same trust model as heartbeat / supply-drop).

get.description:
Admin: aggregate counts + last 20 gifts.

⚠️ Nothing calls this any more — the dashboard's Inactivity-gifts panel
was removed 2026-09. It is kept deliberately, for the same reason
INACTIVITY_GIFT_ENABLED is a constant rather than deleted code: this is
the only view onto the ~38k unclaimed rows still queued, and it is what
you would want back the moment the gift is re-enabled. Curl it directly.

post.description:
Admin: queue a one-off balance grant for ONE device (support
compensation). The player's next app launch claims it and shows the
BALANCE GIFT card — no app update needed, any shipped build.

Body: { "device_id": "<hex>", "amount": 4000,
        "allow_unknown": false }

The reply echoes the device's last_seen / app_version / mirrored balance
and any grant already queued for them — read it before walking away, the
same way `forced_update_impact` exists to be read: a mistyped device id
is otherwise a grant that silently never arrives, and a re-run is a
second payout on the next launch.

get.description:
Admin: the last 50 hand-made grants and whether each was collected.

`claimed_at` is the proof of delivery — it is stamped by the player's own
app on the launch that banked the money.

post.description:
Everything the referral screen needs in one call: the caller's own code,
their referred friends (agent portrait + level, no usernames), and the
total of any unclaimed milestone rewards. Runs the milestone sweep as a
side effect, so rewards materialise whenever either party opens the app.

Redeem someone else's code. Business-rule failures return HTTP 200 with
ok=false and a stable machine-readable `error` slug — the client maps those
to localized copy, so never send prose here. Only a malformed request 4xxs.

Drain the caller's unclaimed milestone rewards; the client adds the
returned total to its local balance.

Marks claimed BEFORE the client banks the money, matching
/api/inactivity-gift/claim. If the client dies in that window the reward is
lost rather than duplicated — the right way round for soft currency, and a
window of milliseconds.

Everything the Friends tab needs in one call: the caller's own code,
their friends (agent portrait + level + presence), and both directions of
pending requests.

Send a friend request by code. Business-rule failures return HTTP 200
with ok=false and a stable slug the client localizes — never prose.

Accept or decline an incoming request. Both sides are re-checked
against FRIEND_MAX here, not just at request time — either party could
have filled up while the request sat pending.
Withdraw a request the caller sent.

Either party may remove; the single friendship row goes away for both.
No notification — being un-friended isn't something to push about.

Mint a gift for a friend.

Addressed by friendship id, like every other friends endpoint — the caller
never learns the recipient's device_id. The sender pays NOTHING: the value
is rolled here and granted out of thin air, which is what keeps this a
faucet rather than a trade between two players.

Business-rule failures return HTTP 200 with a stable slug:
`already_sent` (they still have an unopened one from us), `daily_limit`,
`not_found` (not our friendship).

Open a gift and return the dollar value the client should materialise.

Marked opened BEFORE the client banks anything, same discipline as
/api/referral/claim: a crash in that window loses the gift rather than
duplicating it, which is the right way round for soft currency.

The UPDATE is the atomic claim — two taps that race both reach the SELECT,
but only one can move `opened_at` off NULL.

Drain this device's queued friendship-star rewards.

Marks them claimed BEFORE replying, same discipline as
/api/referral/claim: a crash in that window loses the reward rather than
duplicating it, which is the right way round for soft currency. The client
must therefore bank a non-zero response unconditionally.

Mint a new friend code and invalidate the old one.

Also drops every pending INCOMING request, because those were addressed to
the code being burned. This is the whole point of the button: someone who
posted their code publicly can cut off the resulting flood in one tap.
Existing friendships are untouched.

Store this device's profile snapshot (showcase items, rank tiers,
cosmetics) so friends can view it. Opaque to the server — it's rendered
entirely by the client's existing profile popup — so it's stored verbatim
and only size-checked.

Fetch one friend's profile, addressed by friendship id. Lazy — the
friends LIST only needs level/agent/presence, so the heavier snapshot is
only fetched when a row is actually tapped.

Membership in the friendship is verified before anything is returned, and
the friend's device_id is never included in the response.

Give a device a populated friends list, pending requests and referrals.

TWO locks, both required:
  1. The admin bearer token — same one every /api/admin/ route uses.
  2. The `dev_seed_enabled` flag.

The token is the one that matters. This endpoint writes `users` rows and
queues referral reward rows, so while it was flag-only it was an
unauthenticated write open to anyone who knew the path — a data-pollution
and DB-growth vector, and (while the forced-update floor was still derived
from client-reported versions) enough fake devices could move that floor
and soft-lock real players. The floor is admin-set now, so that particular
escalation is closed; the pollution and growth reasons stand on their own.

Consequence: the client can no longer call this, because shipping the admin
token in the APK would leak it to anyone with `jadx`. Seed from a terminal
instead — see the curl in CLAUDE.md. `FriendsService.seedSocialTestData`
still exists and now simply fails closed (401), so skip-intro and the dev
button degrade to doing nothing rather than needing code changes.

Delete every `testfriend_*` / `testref_*` device and everything hanging
off them, across every table that carries a device id.

Run this before shipping the update so launch analytics aren't polluted by
seeded requests, referrals and users. Also flips `dev_seed_enabled` off so
nothing can re-seed afterwards.

LIKE patterns escape the underscore — an unescaped `_` is a single-char
wildcard in SQL and would widen the match.

Test-only: age a seeded friend request so the relative-time label
("2d ago") can actually be exercised. Requests are always created with
created_at = now, so there is otherwise no way to see anything but "Today".

Deliberately narrow: admin token required AND the sender must be a
`testfriend_` device, so this can never touch a real player's request.
Safe to delete once the friends UI is signed off.

get.description: Admin: is anyone actually using this?

Admin: the friend-gift funnel, for the dashboard's Gifts tab.

The summary counters on /api/friends/stats are the "is anyone using this"
glance; this is the detailed view. Both read the same table, so they can
differ in detail but never in value.

Every money figure is IN-GAME dollars — gifts are minted, so none of this
costs anything real.

"Today" means the current UTC day, matching the window the daily cap itself
uses (_gift_day_start). Any other definition would make `senders_at_cap`
disagree with what players are actually being allowed to send.

post.description:
Replace this device's opt-out set.

Body: `{device_id, disabled: ["supply_drop", ...]}`. Anything absent from
`disabled` is (re-)enabled, so the client can POST its whole current state
and never has to diff. Unknown type names are dropped rather than 400'd —
an older client sending a type we've since renamed shouldn't fail the
whole save.

get.description: Admin: how the referral funnel is performing.

post.description: Record a case battle creation or join. No body fields required.

Track a minigame bet or cash-out for ROI analytics.
Body: {game, type:'bet'|'cashout', value:$}. Money accumulated in CENTS.

Zero the ROI counters (bet/cashout × count/cents) for ONE game, leaving
every other game untouched. For "plinko" this also clears the legacy bare
counter AND all four per-mode variants so the whole dashboard row resets.
Admin only. Body: {"game": "plinko"}.

Record a save-load failure for a device. Body fields:
device_id, app_version, stage, error_type, error_message,
primary_size, backup_size, primary_exists, backup_exists,
primary_head (first ~256 bytes of the primary file, base64 or text)

get.description: Admin: list recent save-load failures. Requires Bearer token.

post.description:
Wipe the analytics EVENT tables — written to reset counts to 0 at
production launch (existing rows were emulators / re-installs /
pre-launch testing).

Wipes: ad_events, ad_fallback_events, feedback, save_load_failures,
notification_log, device_counters.

⚠️ Keeps (2026-10-06, deliberately): `counters`, `users`, `cooldowns`,
`inactivity_gifts`, `fcm_tokens`. It used to wipe the first four too, and
`counters` holds every remote flag: one call disarmed the forced-update
floor, cleared every game kill-switch and referral amount, and reset
`pro_agent_legacy_cutoff_ts`, which the next /api/flags read then
re-stamped to "now", silently moving the pro-agent grandfather cutoff.
`inactivity_gifts` holds unpaid hand-made make-good grants. None of that is
analytics, and none of it can be recovered once deleted.

Zero the ROI counters for ONE game (and its per-mode variants) without
touching any other game or counter. Body: { "game": "plinko" }.

Deletes every counter whose key starts with the literal "<game>_" prefix —
for plinko that is plinko_bet_cents, plinko_cashout_count, and the variant
keys plinko_12_high_bet_cents, etc. `game` must be a bare base-game name
(letters only, present in GAME_KEYS), so this can never be aimed at an
arbitrary key pattern. Returns the exact keys removed for verification.

Add a device to the silent-mute list and wipe their existing
analytics footprint in one call. After this:
  - Future heartbeat/purchase/ad-watch/ad-fallback/save-load
    POSTs from this device_id return 200 OK without writing anything.
  - Their `users` row + event rows are deleted so the dashboard drops
    them immediately. Conversion / aggregated totals re-compute next
    request.
  - The in-memory blacklist cache is busted so the next request
    from the device hits the new state without waiting 30s.

Body: { "device_id": "<hex>", "reason": "<freetext, optional>" }

get.description: The one active job, or null.

post.description:
What the brake is doing (shown by the status endpoint), and the
scheduled -> running step when the brake lets a job start.
Hand the broadcaster its next batch of phones.
A batch is done: count it, prune the dead tokens, release the lease.

Queue a broadcast (or, with dry_run, only count it). Returns at once;
the broadcaster starts it when the API has room.

Body:
  title, body (required) — <= 100 / <= 500 chars
  type        — data.type for tap routing (default "announcement";
                "update_available" opens the store listing)
  translations — {"ru": {"title": ..., "body": ...}}; unlisted languages
                 get the base copy

                [0, 10] now and [10, 100] later reach disjoint phones.
  pace        — phones per second, default 30, max 100 (alias:
                rate_per_second)
  ttl_hours   — default 72
  send_after  — epoch seconds; not before this
  brake       — per-job overrides of BROADCAST_BRAKE_DEFAULTS
  dry_run     — count only; also shows whether the API could take it now

Send the copy to the admin's own phone only, once per language (English
plus every translation), through the same sender a real broadcast uses.

get.description:
The active job, else the most recent one (or `?job_id=`). Read from the
database, so it answers even while the broadcaster is restarting.
The last 20 jobs, newest first.

post.description: Change a live job's `pace` or `brake` without a redeploy.

get.description: Total registered users + new in the last 24h. No auth, cached 60s.

Public read of client-visible feature flags. Cached 60s server-side.
Returns a mixed-type payload: bool flags as true/false, int flags as
raw integers.

`?platform=ios|android` selects which population the forced-update floor
is computed from. **Absent means android**, so every client already in the
wild — none of which send the parameter — gets byte-identical behaviour to
before this parameter existed. Only the flag `min_required_version` varies
by platform; every other value in the payload is global.

post.description:
Toggle client-visible feature flags. Admin token required.

Body: { "<flag_key>": true|false|int, ... }
Bool flags accept any truthy/falsy value; int flags accept an integer
that gets clamped to [min, max] defined in `_INT_FLAGS`. Unknown keys
return 400 so typos don't silently no-op. Returns the new full flag
state (post-clamp for int flags so the admin sees what was persisted).

get.description:
Diagnostic: can this server's service account reach `package` on the
Play Developer API? Read-only, writes nothing.

Probes subscriptionsv2 with a deliberately invalid token. The status code
separates "no permission" from "permission fine, token just isn't real":
  401 -> credential/scope problem
  403 -> SA has no access to THIS package (or API not enabled on the project)
  404 -> token not found => ACCESS OK
  400 -> malformed token   => ACCESS OK

post.description:
The app's Play Integrity token (or why it couldn't get one).
`{device_id, app_version, token}` or `{device_id, app_version, error}`.
Always answers `{ok: true}` once the body is valid — report-only, so
there is nothing for a client to branch on, and a modded client learns
nothing about what we saw.

get.description:
What the Play Integrity reports say, over devices checked in the last
`days` (max 90). One GROUP BY per breakdown, so it is cheap at any size.

How to read it: `app_verdict` PLAY_RECOGNIZED is the real Play build;
UNRECOGNIZED_VERSION is a modified or re-signed copy (the mod);
UNEVALUATED means Play couldn't judge (usually no device integrity).
`hash_ok` 0 on a decoded row means the token was made for another device
or day — a replayed token.

Can this server's service account decode Play Integrity tokens for the
app? Decodes a deliberately invalid token: 400 means Google accepted our
credential and rejected the token (ACCESS OK); 401/403 means the
credential, the project link or the API enablement is wrong.

Where new installs get to, over installs whose funnel started in the
last `days` (max 60), optionally one app language (`lang=en`).

Only FRESH installs count: the funnel row must start within a few hours
of the device's first heartbeat, which drops an old install that went
through Reset Account on 1.1.5 (its setup screens show again).

Per step: how many reached it, the median / quartile seconds after the
setup screens, and — over installs at least 2 days old — how many came
back a day or more after their first heartbeat, split by whether they
reached the step. `last_step_of_leavers` is, for those 2-day-old installs
that never came back, the last step they reached: where the first session
ended. A plain `def` on purpose (one SELECT, then Python over ~100k rows).
